title: Communication style quiz: assertive, passive, aggressive or passive-aggressive? Free test — cv.cm
description: Free communication style quiz: 12 everyday situations show whether you lean assertive, passive, aggressive or passive-aggressive, with tips for speaking up clearly and kindly. No sign-up.
lede: Do you say what you need, keep the peace, push hard or hint? Pick how you'd really react in 12 everyday situations at work, at home and with friends to find your main communication style.
about: Communication skills courses often describe four styles. Assertive people say what they think and need, clearly and respectfully, and listen to others too. Passive people put others first and keep quiet to avoid conflict. Aggressive people get their point across forcefully, sometimes at others' expense. Passive-aggressive people seem to go along but show their frustration indirectly, through sarcasm, sulking or quiet resistance. Most of us use all four depending on the situation; this quiz shows which one you fall back on most.

Each question offers one answer for each style, and your result names the style you chose most, with all four scores. There are no bad people here, only habits, and every style can be shifted toward assertive with practice. The quiz was written for cv.cm from this common four-style model. It is a starting point for reflection, not a professional assessment. If you'd like to look at disagreements in more depth, try the conflict style quiz on this site.

faq.q: What are the four communication styles?
faq.a: Assertive (clear and respectful), passive (avoiding conflict by staying quiet), aggressive (forceful, winning at others' expense) and passive-aggressive (indirect frustration, such as sarcasm or silent treatment).
Assertive communication is usually the most effective, because you say what you need while respecting the other person. But it's a skill, not a personality, and anyone can learn it.
Most people use different styles in different places, say passive at work and aggressive with family. Look at your two highest scores and think about where each shows up.
No. The quiz is scored in your browser and nothing is sent or stored.

items.q: A coworker keeps taking credit for your ideas. You…
options: Talk to them privately and say it needs to stop
Let it go; it's not worth a fight
Call them out in front of everyone
Make a pointed joke about it in the next meeting

items.q: Your friend is always late. You…
options: Tell them off when they finally arrive
Say "no worries" and then turn up late yourself next time
Wait without saying anything
Tell them it bothers you and suggest a fix

items.q: Your order arrives wrong at a restaurant. You…
options: Eat it anyway
Complain loudly and demand to see the manager
Politely ask them to fix it
Say it's fine, then leave a bad review

items.q: Someone cuts in front of you in line. You…
options: Sigh loudly so they hear
Say, "Excuse me, the line starts back there"
Say nothing
Tell them exactly what you think of them

items.q: Your partner forgot something important to you. You…
options: Tell them you felt hurt and why
Start an argument right away
Go quiet and wait for them to notice
Pretend it doesn't matter

items.q: In a meeting, you disagree with the plan. You…
options: Agree out loud, then drag your feet
Keep quiet and go along with it
Shoot the idea down hard
Share your concern and suggest an alternative

items.q: A roommate leaves dirty dishes again. You…
options: Leave them a furious note
Pile the dishes on their bed
Ask to agree on a rule together
Wash them yourself, again

items.q: Someone asks for a favor you don't have time for. You…
options: Say yes and stay up late doing it
Say no kindly and explain why
Tell them they're always asking too much
Say yes, then do it half-heartedly

items.q: You get feedback you think is unfair. You…
options: Ask for examples and give your side calmly
Say thanks, then complain about it to others
Accept it and feel bad
Argue back on the spot

items.q: When you're upset with someone, they usually find out…
options: Rarely; I keep it inside
Immediately and loudly
Through my tone and the cold shoulder
Because I tell them, calmly

items.q: A friend keeps interrupting you. You…
options: Stop talking and roll your eyes
Let them talk and give up on your point
Say, "Hang on, let me finish"
Talk over them, louder

items.q: Which sentence sounds most like you?
options: "I say what I think, and if people can't handle it, that's on them."
"I can say no and still be kind."
"Fine. Whatever. It's not like my opinion matters."
"I'd rather keep the peace than cause a fuss."

assertive.name: Assertive
assertive.body: You usually say what you think and need, clearly and respectfully, and you listen to the other side too. That earns trust and solves problems before they grow. Keep it up, and remember that being assertive includes knowing when to let small things go.

passive.name: Passive
passive.body: You often put other people's needs first and stay quiet to keep the peace. People find you easy to be around, but your own needs can get lost and resentment can build. Try small steps: say no to one small request, or share one opinion a day. Your voice matters too.

aggressive.name: Aggressive
aggressive.body: You speak your mind forcefully and don't back down, which can get results fast. But it can leave others feeling run over, and they may stop telling you things. Try pausing before you react, using "I" instead of "you" statements and asking a question before making your point. Your honesty is a strength when it comes with respect.

passiveaggressive.name: Passive-aggressive
passiveaggressive.body: You often go along with things on the surface but let your frustration out indirectly, through sarcasm, silence or quiet resistance. That's usually a sign you don't feel safe saying it straight. Try naming what bothers you early, while it's still small: "I'm annoyed that…" works better than a sigh. People can't fix what they don't know about.
